A free first session

Here's why most young pitchers stop adding velocity, even when they throw all year and show up to every lesson.
The number on the gun isn't stuck because the kid stopped working. Most of these kids are working harder than ever. It's stuck because nobody has measured what's actually capping it.
Velocity is built on how an athlete moves. The hips, the trunk, the timing of the whole chain. When there's a limiter buried in that movement and no one finds it, every extra throw just grooves the same pattern a little deeper. The kid isn't getting closer to the next tier of velo. They're getting more efficient at the ceiling they already have. That's the quiet trap, and it's why effort and frustration keep climbing while the number sits still.
Most throwing programs never catch this, because they aren't built to look. Same drills for every arm. More volume, more bullpens, more weighted balls, and a hope that something clicks.
ISP is built the opposite way. Every athlete starts with a movement screen and a full throwing evaluation, so we can see the specific thing holding the velocity back, whether that's a mechanical breakdown or a movement pattern that needs work. From there we build an individualized throwing plan around that athlete's actual needs, not a template. Then we reassess every month and adjust, so the plan keeps pace with the kid instead of going stale.
Here's what that does once the real limiter starts getting trained. The gun starts climbing again. A faster, cleaner arm shows up at the next outing, which means hitters the kid couldn't beat last season start swinging under it. That turns into more innings and a bigger role on the staff. Coaches and crosscheckers start writing the number down. And that number, the one that finally moved, is exactly what travels to showcases, lands in front of recruiters, and turns into the recruiting conversation a family has been hoping for since the kid first picked up a ball.
This is the same process behind 1500+ athletes trained, 100+ MLB Draft Picks, and 6 first-round picks. Results at that volume don't come from talent showing up by accident. They come from a system that gets repeated, athlete after athlete.
One more thing worth saying plainly: chasing velocity and protecting the arm aren't opposites here. Cleaning up how an athlete moves raises the number and lowers the injury risk at the same time. You don't have to choose.

Most baseball parents believe they're stuck with a choice. Push the kid for more velocity and risk the arm, or play it safe and watch the number stall. One or the other.
That trade-off isn't real. Velocity and arm injuries trace back to the same root: how the athlete moves. When a pitcher moves inefficiently, two things happen at once. Power leaks out of the chain, so the velo caps. And the arm starts compensating for what the body isn't doing, which is exactly the stress that leads to injury. Same flaw, two symptoms.
So the fix isn't "throw harder and hope" or "back off and stay safe." It's cleaning up the movement, which raises the number and takes load off the arm at the same time.
That's why ISP doesn't hand out a generic throwing program. Every athlete starts with a movement screen and a full throwing evaluation. For arms that are still maturing or already at risk, we have a Mechanical Patterning track built to add velocity by moving better, not by piling on volume. The plan fits the arm in front of us, and we reassess it every month.
Here's what that looks like for the kid. The movement gets cleaner, so the gun starts climbing again. And because the arm isn't fighting itself anymore, it holds up instead of breaking down. That means more innings, fewer days lost to soreness, and a bigger role coaches can actually rely on. An available arm with a rising number is the one that travels to showcases and ends up in front of recruiters.
This is the process behind 1500+ athletes trained, 100+ MLB Draft Picks, and 6 first-round picks.

Most baseball parents are quietly carrying a choice they think they have to make. Push the kid to throw harder and gain velocity, and accept that the arm might pay for it. Or protect the arm, hold him back, and watch the number sit still while other kids pass him. Velo or health. Pick one.
That choice is a myth, and it's costing families both things they want.
Velocity and arm injuries are not separate problems with separate solutions. They grow from the same root: how the athlete moves. When a pitcher's movement is inefficient, the power that should come from the hips and trunk never fully shows up, so the velocity caps out. And the arm, sensing the body isn't doing its share, starts working overtime to make up the difference. That extra load, throw after throw, is exactly the stress that turns into soreness and then into real injury. The flat radar number and the sore elbow aren't two problems. They're one flaw showing up in two places.
Once you see that, the fix stops being a gamble. You don't throw harder and hope the arm survives. You don't back off and hope the velo comes on its own. You clean up the movement, and the number goes up while the load on the arm goes down. At the same time.
That's the whole reason ISP doesn't run kids through a one-size throwing program. Every athlete starts with a movement screen and a full throwing evaluation, so we can see what that specific arm needs. Advanced, physically mature pitchers with a training background go into Velocity Development, where intent drives bigger gains. Athletes who haven't matured yet, who've had a prior arm injury, or whose current mechanics put them at risk go into Mechanical Patterning, a track designed to add velocity through moving more efficiently rather than through piling on volume. Either way, the plan is built around the athlete and reassessed every single month, so it adjusts as the kid grows instead of going stale.
Here's what it adds up to on the field. The movement gets cleaner, so the gun starts climbing again. Because the arm isn't compensating anymore, it holds up under a real workload instead of breaking down. That turns into more innings and fewer days lost to a sore arm, which turns into a bigger, more dependable role on the staff. Coaches start trusting him with the ball in games that matter. And an arm that's both available and getting faster is the exact profile that travels to showcases, lands in front of crosscheckers, and turns into the recruiting conversation a family has been hoping for.
This is the same process behind 1500+ athletes trained, 100+ MLB Draft Picks, and 6 first-round picks. Numbers like that, across that many arms, don't come from getting lucky with talent. They come from a system that solves the right problem and gets repeated.

ad-1-long.primaryText.text:
Here's why most young pitchers stop adding velocity, even when they throw all year and show up to every lesson.
The number on the gun isn't stuck because the kid stopped working. Most of these kids are working harder than ever. It's stuck because nobody has measured what's actually capping it.
Velocity is built on how an athlete moves. The hips, the trunk, the timing of the whole chain. When there's a limiter buried in that movement and no one finds it, every extra throw just grooves the same pattern a little deeper. The kid isn't getting closer to the next tier of velo. They're getting more efficient at the ceiling they already have. That's the quiet trap, and it's why effort and frustration keep climbing while the number sits still.
Most throwing programs never catch this, because they aren't built to look. Same drills for every arm. More volume, more bullpens, more weighted balls, and a hope that something clicks.
ISP is built the opposite way. Every athlete starts with a movement screen and a full throwing evaluation, so we can see the specific thing holding the velocity back, whether that's a mechanical breakdown or a movement pattern that needs work. From there we build an individualized throwing plan around that athlete's actual needs, not a template. Then we reassess every month and adjust, so the plan keeps pace with the kid instead of going stale.
Here's what that does once the real limiter starts getting trained. The gun starts climbing again. A faster, cleaner arm shows up at the next outing, which means hitters the kid couldn't beat last season start swinging under it. That turns into more innings and a bigger role on the staff. Coaches and crosscheckers start writing the number down. And that number, the one that finally moved, is exactly what travels to showcases, lands in front of recruiters, and turns into the recruiting conversation a family has been hoping for since the kid first picked up a ball.
This is the same process behind 1500+ athletes trained, 100+ MLB Draft Picks, and 6 first-round picks. Results at that volume don't come from talent showing up by accident. They come from a system that gets repeated, athlete after athlete.
One more thing worth saying plainly: chasing velocity and protecting the arm aren't opposites here. Cleaning up how an athlete moves raises the number and lowers the injury risk at the same time. You don't have to choose.

ad-2-medium.primaryText.text:
Most baseball parents believe they're stuck with a choice. Push the kid for more velocity and risk the arm, or play it safe and watch the number stall. One or the other.
That trade-off isn't real. Velocity and arm injuries trace back to the same root: how the athlete moves. When a pitcher moves inefficiently, two things happen at once. Power leaks out of the chain, so the velo caps. And the arm starts compensating for what the body isn't doing, which is exactly the stress that leads to injury. Same flaw, two symptoms.
So the fix isn't "throw harder and hope" or "back off and stay safe." It's cleaning up the movement, which raises the number and takes load off the arm at the same time.
That's why ISP doesn't hand out a generic throwing program. Every athlete starts with a movement screen and a full throwing evaluation. For arms that are still maturing or already at risk, we have a Mechanical Patterning track built to add velocity by moving better, not by piling on volume. The plan fits the arm in front of us, and we reassess it every month.
Here's what that looks like for the kid. The movement gets cleaner, so the gun starts climbing again. And because the arm isn't fighting itself anymore, it holds up instead of breaking down. That means more innings, fewer days lost to soreness, and a bigger role coaches can actually rely on. An available arm with a rising number is the one that travels to showcases and ends up in front of recruiters.
This is the process behind 1500+ athletes trained, 100+ MLB Draft Picks, and 6 first-round picks.

ad-2-long.primaryText.text:
Most baseball parents are quietly carrying a choice they think they have to make. Push the kid to throw harder and gain velocity, and accept that the arm might pay for it. Or protect the arm, hold him back, and watch the number sit still while other kids pass him. Velo or health. Pick one.
That choice is a myth, and it's costing families both things they want.
Velocity and arm injuries are not separate problems with separate solutions. They grow from the same root: how the athlete moves. When a pitcher's movement is inefficient, the power that should come from the hips and trunk never fully shows up, so the velocity caps out. And the arm, sensing the body isn't doing its share, starts working overtime to make up the difference. That extra load, throw after throw, is exactly the stress that turns into soreness and then into real injury. The flat radar number and the sore elbow aren't two problems. They're one flaw showing up in two places.
Once you see that, the fix stops being a gamble. You don't throw harder and hope the arm survives. You don't back off and hope the velo comes on its own. You clean up the movement, and the number goes up while the load on the arm goes down. At the same time.
That's the whole reason ISP doesn't run kids through a one-size throwing program. Every athlete starts with a movement screen and a full throwing evaluation, so we can see what that specific arm needs. Advanced, physically mature pitchers with a training background go into Velocity Development, where intent drives bigger gains. Athletes who haven't matured yet, who've had a prior arm injury, or whose current mechanics put them at risk go into Mechanical Patterning, a track designed to add velocity through moving more efficiently rather than through piling on volume. Either way, the plan is built around the athlete and reassessed every single month, so it adjusts as the kid grows instead of going stale.
Here's what it adds up to on the field. The movement gets cleaner, so the gun starts climbing again. Because the arm isn't compensating anymore, it holds up under a real workload instead of breaking down. That turns into more innings and fewer days lost to a sore arm, which turns into a bigger, more dependable role on the staff. Coaches start trusting him with the ball in games that matter. And an arm that's both available and getting faster is the exact profile that travels to showcases, lands in front of crosscheckers, and turns into the recruiting conversation a family has been hoping for.
This is the same process behind 1500+ athletes trained, 100+ MLB Draft Picks, and 6 first-round picks. Numbers like that, across that many arms, don't come from getting lucky with talent. They come from a system that solves the right problem and gets repeated.

It's the same thing happening on purpose, over and over, leaving the same fingerprints.
So the honest question isn't "is your kid talented enough to belong on that wall." It's "what's the process, and does it work on a normal athlete." Here's the answer, and it's two things working together.
The first is that ISP develops the whole athlete, not just the throw. A lot of places only work on the arm and the delivery. ISP starts underneath that, with movement, strength, and explosive power, and then layers the individualized throwing plan on top of a body that can actually produce and support more velocity. You're not refining a throw in isolation. You're building the engine the throw comes from.
The second is what keeps it working. The plan doesn't get set once and run on autopilot. Every month, the athlete is reassessed and the plan gets adjusted to where the kid actually is now. That's the difference between a program that produces a spike and then stalls, and one that keeps producing season after season. The monthly loop is why the results don't run out.
Put those together and you have something that has nothing to do with being born gifted. It's a repeatable process, and a repeatable process works on whoever runs it. That's why it built draft picks, and it's the same reason it can move the needle for a 14-year-old who's never been measured in his life.
Here's what it looks like for that kid. When the whole athlete gets developed and the plan keeps adjusting, the velocity doesn't just jump once and fade. It climbs and holds. A faster arm that's also durable earns more innings instead of losing weeks to soreness, and more innings means a bigger, more dependable role on the staff. That role generates film, and film of a kid throwing harder and holding it deep into games is exactly the profile that travels to showcases, gets in front of crosscheckers, and turns into the recruiting conversation a family has been hoping for since the kid first picked up a ball.
